What a German notary does

German law requires notarial form for important contracts and declarations. The notary drafts, explains and notarises. Unlike a notary public in common-law countries, a German notary is a legally trained holder of a public office.

Real estate

Buying and selling a house, apartment or land. Land charge for financing. Transfers within the family.

Read more

Inheritance

Wills and inheritance contracts. What applies without a will, what the compulsory portion is, how to obtain a certificate of inheritance.

Read more

Gifts

Transferring assets during your lifetime, secured by a right of residence, usufruct or reclaim rights.

Read more

Powers of attorney

Lasting power of attorney, living will and guardianship directive: who decides when you no longer can.

Read more

Family

Marriage contracts, separation and divorce agreements, adoption, acknowledgement of paternity.

Read more

Companies

Forming a GmbH, transferring shares, commercial register. Online notarisation by video where permitted.

Read more

Certifications and Switzerland

Certified signatures and copies. Documents for Swiss authorities and other countries.

The notary

Kai-Christoph Stadler

Notary with seat in Bad Säckingen since 2018. Previously state notary and probate judge in Furtwangen and Donaueschingen; law studies in Konstanz and Freiburg.

The notary holds a public office. He advises all parties equally, is bound by law and sworn to confidentiality. He may not refuse an official act without good reason.

How it works

Four steps, the same for every matter. You sign nothing that has not been explained to you first.

  1. Enquiry

    You call, write or complete a questionnaire. The office clarifies what is needed and which documents are required.

  2. Draft

    The notary drafts the contract or declaration. You receive the draft in advance to read.

  3. Notarisation

    At the appointment the notary reads the deed aloud, explains it and answers questions. Then everyone signs.

  4. Completion

    The office handles the land register, commercial register and authorities and informs you when everything is done.

Procedure in detail, questionnaires and document checklists

What an appointment costs

Notary fees are fixed by the German Court and Notary Costs Act (GNotKG). They depend on the value of the transaction, not on the time spent, and are identical at every notary in Germany.

Advice connected with a notarisation is included in the fee. We tell you the expected costs in advance.

How the fees work

On the Swiss border

Bad Säckingen lies on the Rhine, opposite Stein in the canton of Aargau. Many clients live, work or hold assets on both sides of the border.

  • Property purchases in Germany by buyers from Switzerland
  • Estates with assets in both countries
  • Certifications and apostilles for Swiss authorities

Documents for Switzerland

Explained in plain terms

Notarial deeds use words that do not occur in everyday life: Auflassung, Vollzug, Pflichtteil, Nießbrauch. At the appointment the notary explains each of them. If you want to read up beforehand, the glossary covers the most important terms in English.

To the glossary

Good to know

  • Bring a valid passport or identity card to every appointment.
  • If you do not understand German sufficiently, an interpreter is required by law. The office helps you find one.
  • If you cannot attend in person, you can be represented. Ask in advance.
